instructions:
Below is a draft essay. Revise it so that it reads as if a US grade 8 student wrote it in class for a timed writing test. Keep the position it argues and keep it at about 336 words. The file must contain only the revised essay.

A measurement tool compared the draft with essays that students wrote on other assignments. Use its report when you revise:

Tone check against human essay writing (333 words). Distance from the human centre: 0.34 (1.0 is typical for a human text).
Every measure is inside the range that covers the middle 80% of human texts. Nothing to change on tone.
These are ranges, not targets. Change wording only where the change also makes the text more specific or more honest.

Draft:

Dear Principal,

I am writing about the cell phone policy you are reconsidering. I believe Policy 1 is the better choice. Students should be allowed to bring phones to school and use them during lunch and other free times, as long as the phones stay off during class.

The first reason is safety. Many parents want to reach their children in an emergency, and students need a way to call home if they feel sick, miss the bus, or have a change of plans after school. If something serious happened at school, a phone could let a student contact family or emergency services right away. Banning phones completely would take that away from everyone just to prevent a few distractions.

The second reason is that phones help students manage their lives. Many of us have jobs, sports practices, or younger siblings to pick up. A quick text at lunch to a coach or a parent can sort out a schedule problem before it becomes a bigger one. Phones also hold calendars, reminders, and school apps that help us stay organized.

Third, Policy 1 teaches responsibility. Once we graduate, nobody will take our phones away at work or college. We will have to decide for ourselves when it is appropriate to use them. Letting students practice that self-control now, with clear rules about class time, prepares us better than a total ban that simply removes the choice.

Some people worry that students will break the rule and use phones in class. That concern is fair, but the answer is to enforce the rule, not to punish every student. Teachers could collect a phone from anyone caught using it during class, and repeat offenders could lose the privilege. Most students would follow the rule if they knew they could check their phones at lunch.

Policy 2 would also be hard to enforce and would likely lead to students hiding phones anyway. Policy 1 is fair, practical, and realistic. I hope you will choose it.

Sincerely,
A Concerned Student
